Classification of stellar spectra by features controlled mainly by temperature and also by surface gravity and composition. The O-B-A-F-G-K-M temperature sequence does not mean a corresponding sequence in bulk hydrogen abundance.

A stellar spectral category based on gravity-sensitive line widths and ratios, distinguishing supergiants, giants and dwarfs at comparable spectral temperature. The stellar temperature sequence O, B, A, F, G, K, M, with numerical subclasses approximately from hotter 0 to cooler 9 within each letter class. A separate luminosity class describes gravity-sensitive spectral differences.

A plot of stellar magnitude against a colour index. It is an observational counterpart of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, but converting colour to effective temperature and magnitude to luminosity requires calibration, extinction and distance information. A coeval population's main-sequence turnoff helps estimate its stellar age.

An RR Lyrae star is a short-period pulsating evolved star used as a distance tracer in old populations. Its calibrated luminosity depends on composition and photometric band; infrared period-luminosity-metallicity relations are especially useful. extinction, crowding, mode identification and calibration remain important.

Time-dependent stellar phenomena such as starspots and chromospheric emission that can change brightness and spectral-line shapes, complicating radial-velocity planet searches.

Stellar variability that contaminates a planetary radial-velocity or photometric signal. Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Neutrino astronomy infers properties of astronomical sources from detected neutrino reactions. Solar neutrino detection probes ongoing stellar nuclear fusion; the SN 1987A neutrino burst probes a brief episode of core-collapse supernova evolution. A detector observes reaction products, so source inference depends on cross sections, neutrino flavor, thresholds and detection efficiency.

Kamiokande

Words: 321 Articles: 1
Neutrino astronomy OurBigBook.com
Kamiokande, associated with Masatoshi Koshiba, was an underground water Cherenkov detector viewed by photomultipliers. Improved water purity and reduced background enabled solar neutrino observations. A concentration of reconstructed recoil directions toward the Sun distinguished a source signal above an approximately direction-independent background.[ref]
For solar neutrinos, electron elastic scattering supplies a directional recoil, with different cross sections for active neutrino flavors. Neither the Homestake experiment deficit nor the SN 1987A neutrino burst alone established neutrino oscillation; later evidence compared complementary channels and propagation effects.[ref]

Water Cherenkov neutrino reconstruction (ti​≃t0​+cn​∣ri​−r0​∣)

Words: 247
Kamiokande OurBigBook.com
Water Cherenkov neutrino reconstruction infers a vertex, time and charged particle direction from photomultiplier pulses. The 1987 analysis recorded charge and timing, calibrated with decaying muons and source-produced gamma rays, and rejected outer-detector activity and events following muons.[ref]
In an ideal point-flash approximation, a light source at r0​ and time t0​ gives the displayed travel-time relation at sensor ri​ in a medium of refractive index n. Subtracting two times eliminates t0​. With a chosen constant n=1.33 and path lengths 3m and 6m, the arrival-time difference is n(3m)/c≃13.31ns. These are synthetic inputs, not detector measurements. Several sensors constrain the vertex; an extended moving track requires the light-emission position and time along that track as well.
For a charged particle moving at v=βc, the Cherenkov cone angle satisfies cosθC​=1/(nβ) when nβ>1. With β≃1 and the illustrative n=1.33, θC​≃41.25∘. The geometrical cone carries track-direction information; electron deflections and the spread of emission positions broaden the observed pattern. The neutrino itself does not draw the light cone.
A Cherenkov radiation threshold and an analysis threshold are different constraints. For a fixed n, an electron must exceed TC​=me​c2[(1−n−2)−1/2−1]. With me​c2=0.511MeV and the chosen n=1.33, this gives about 0.264MeV. Recording and selecting a useful event requires much more light: the 1987 detector's trigger accepted 8.5MeV electrons with 50% efficiency.[ref]

Orbital dynamics gives the most direct stellar masses: a resolved binary orbit and distance determine the relative semimajor axis, and Kepler's third law gives the total mass. The barycentric size or radial-velocity amplitude ratio gives individual masses. An eclipsing binary inclination removes the sine-cubed projection factor from spectroscopic masses; a single-lined binary mass function alone does not uniquely determine both masses. Surface-gravity/radius and stellar-track estimates are model-dependent and are calibrated against dynamical binary measurements.

The spin of a star about its axis, which can be solid-body rotation or vary through the interior. Angular momentum transport and rotational mixing can change the stellar composition profile and available fuel. An observed surface rotation rate does not determine the entire interior profile.

In a steady axisymmetric star, a torque due to Reynolds stress, Maxwell stress tensor or viscosity must balance advection of specific angular momentum by stellar meridional circulation. Writing the nonadvective angular momentum transport flux as FJ​ gives the displayed balance. Thus stresses that maintain differential rotation also drive a meridional response. The stellar thermal-wind balance supplies a separate leading force constraint, not a replacement for this torque equation.

For an approximately spherical ideal gas with constant composition, use ∇ρ=∇p/cs2​−ρ∇S/cp​ to obtain the displayed relation. A barotropic fluid gives cylindrical rotation in this leading balance; the relation does not determine the transport stresses or circulation rate.

A Population III star is a first-generation star formed from essentially metal-free primordial gas. Limited cooling generally raises its characteristic fragmentation mass and favors a more top-heavy initial mass function than in enriched star formation.

A Population II star is an old metal-poor star formed from gas enriched by earlier stellar generations. Metal and dust cooling let enriched gas fragment to lower masses than primordial gas under otherwise comparable conditions.

Integrated spectra can confuse older stellar populations with more metal-rich ones because both can redden the light and change absorption lines. Weak metal lines in a young population dominated by hot bright stars need not indicate low stellar metallicity.

Given a birth-mass distribution and age distribution, an evolutionary state occupies the mass-age set where its starting lifetime has elapsed and its ending lifetime has not. The state number fraction is the probability measure of this set. Initial mass function tail coordinates and the probability integral transform can turn these weighted regions into simple geometric areas.

A phase bounded by mass-dependent lifetimes τa​(M) and τb​(M) occupies τa​(M)<t<τb​(M), clipped to the population age range. Its boundaries can be mapped into uniform probability coordinates to evaluate evolutionary-state fractions.

If a population forms at a constant number rate for duration T and every birth object is retained in the census, its present ages are uniform on [0,T]. A fixed initial mass function with finite mean birth mass also makes constant mass-based star formation rate equivalent to constant number rate.

Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A stellar atmosphere is the outer region that determines the escaping spectrum and matches the interior stellar structure to its radiation boundary conditions. The distribution of radiation from a star with wavelength or frequency, including its continuum and absorption lines. A stellar abundance can be expressed as an elemental or isotopic mass fraction, or as a number ratio to hydrogen. The fraction of total mass in chemical elements heavier than helium, so the hydrogen mass fraction, helium mass fraction and metal mass fraction satisfy X+Y+Z=1. Despite the astronomical name, this includes elements such as carbon and oxygen that are not chemical metals.

When radiative rates compete with or dominate collisions, level populations need statistical equilibrium coupled to radiative transfer, rather than thermal population laws at the local temperature. Spectral line OurBigBook.com
The finite width of a spectral line can arise from finite optical coherence or a distribution of resonance frequencies. lifetime broadening and impact-regime pressure broadening often give Lorentzian line shapes; thermal Doppler broadening gives a Gaussian component. The instrument response must also be included when interpreting a measured spectrum.

Finite interaction time with a spatially confined optical beam gives a finite spectral response width. Its detailed shape depends on the spatial beam profile, particle trajectory and interaction envelope; a duration alone does not imply a universal Lorentzian profile.

Spectral line broadening OurBigBook.com
An ensemble-wide distribution of resonance frequencies, such as velocity-dependent Doppler shifts or spatially varying static-field shifts. The observed profile averages the individual responses. A velocity class need not have the full width of the ensemble's thermal Doppler broadening.

Spectral line broadening OurBigBook.com
Broadening shared by otherwise identical emitters, often described by a common optical coherence time T2​. Exponential field-coherence decay produces a Lorentzian line shape with full angular-frequency width 2/T2​. Population decay, dephasing and collisions can all contribute, with their time constants distinguished.

Spectral line OurBigBook.com
In the absence of additional dephasing, a transition whose excited-state population has lifetime T1​ has a field-coherence decay time 2T1​. Its Lorentzian line shape has angular-frequency half-width 1/(2T1​) and full width 1/T1​. Population decay time, amplitude decay time and linewidth conventions must therefore be distinguished. Extra dephasing shortens the optical coherence time without necessarily changing the population lifetime.

The locus of midpoints between the two sides of a spectral-line profile at equal intensities. Variations with depth or time diagnose changes in line asymmetry; a null result has finite sensitivity.

A pair of neighbouring spectral lines.

Spectral line OurBigBook.com
Collisions and fluctuating neighboring-particle electric fields alter atomic energy levels and coherence times, broadening a spectral line. In a simple impact treatment the coherence-decay rate gives a Lorentzian width of order Γ/(2π); the precise definition of full or half width must be stated. Unlike Doppler broadening, this depends primarily on collision rates and perturber density. In stellar opacity calculations it alters line overlap and the low-opacity windows entering the Rosseland mean opacity.

If phase-randomizing collisions form a Poisson process of mean interval τc​, field correlation survives only when no such collision occurs during the delay. Thus its magnitude decays as e−∣τ∣/τc​. The Wiener-Khinchin theorem gives the normalized Lorentzian line shape
L(ω)=π1​(ω−ω0​)2+(1/τc​)21/τc​​.
(1)
Its full width at half maximum is 2/τc​ in angular frequency or 1/(πτc​) in ordinary frequency. A population lifetime is a different time constant: lifetime-limited amplitude decay at half the population rate introduces the familiar factor of two. The definition of the supplied lifetime must therefore accompany any numerical linewidth.

A Voigt profile is the convolution of a Gaussian distribution and a Cauchy distribution. An emission line is a localized excess of specific intensity above the continuum. Heated chromospheric material can give a line source above the photospheric continuum source. A forbidden emission line is suppressed by the electric-dipole selection rules but can occur through weaker radiative channels such as magnetic-dipole or electric-quadrupole emission. Its relatively long-lived upper atomic level is vulnerable to collisional de-excitation in dense gas. Low-density astrophysical plasmas can therefore display strong forbidden-line emission even when laboratory dense sources do not.

Forbidden emission line OurBigBook.com
In a three-level ion, statistical equilibrium must include collisional coupling between both upper levels as well as excitations from the ground. The upper populations solve a two-by-two linear system when expressed relative to the ground population. Their line ratio is a rational function of electron density, interpolating between a collisionally excited low-density limit and a collisional Boltzmann limit. Closely spaced upper energies reduce temperature sensitivity, but neglecting upper-level collisional mixing can bias the inferred density.

A constant-collision-strength approximation is R≃7.90e32900K/Te​. Increasing temperature strengthens the higher-excitation auroral line and lowers R. An absorption line is a deficit of observed spectral specific intensity relative to the surrounding continuum. For an absorption-dominated LTE source, the Planck function then supplies a smaller line specific intensity. A foreground layer with source below the incident continuum gives another direct transfer description.

The solar corona is the Sun's hot, dilute outer atmosphere. Its optically thin atomic lines diagnose temperature, density and composition through collisional-radiative models and ionization balance. Sun OurBigBook.com
A solar granule is a photospheric convection cell, with relatively hot rising material in its interior and cooler descending material near its edges. Solar granule OurBigBook.com
The evolving cellular intensity pattern on the Sun's photosphere, produced by solar granules. Its radiative appearance and flow pattern are related but are not identical observables. Near-surface horizontal flow can redistribute weak magnetic field into the surrounding intergranular lanes.

An intergranular lane is a region between solar granules, commonly associated with cooler material and descending flow. Sun OurBigBook.com
A solar neutrino is a neutrino produced by a nuclear reaction in the Sun, principally through the proton–proton chain and CNO cycle. Its weak interactions allow it to escape directly from the stellar core. Accounting for neutrino oscillation allows measurements of the different detected flavors to test the nuclear reaction power and rates independently of escaping photons.
Solar neutrino detection
Words: 562 Articles: 2
Solar neutrino OurBigBook.com
Solar neutrino detection asks how an invisible electron neutrino from the Sun becomes a measurable laboratory record. The Homestake experiment stores a reaction product for later counting; Kamiokande records light promptly. The former measures an exposure-integrated rate, whereas the latter can retain event times and statistical source-direction information. These are complementary ways to connect stellar nuclear fusion with neutrino astronomy.
A detector samples a weighted part of a neutrino flux, rather than counting every passing neutrino. For a target population NT​, an ideal reaction rate is
R=NT​∫Emin​∞​ϕe​(E)σe​(E)dE,
(2)
where ϕe​(E) is the differential electron neutrino neutrino flux and σe​(E) is the relevant cross section. A detection efficiency belongs inside the integral if it depends on energy. Two detectors can therefore disagree in raw count rate while observing the same source. Interpreting a deficit requires both a source prediction and a detector response.
Homestake experiment (νe​+37Cl⟶37Ar+e−)
Words: 442 Articles: 1
Solar neutrino detection OurBigBook.com
The Homestake experiment, led by Raymond Davis Jr., used electron neutrino capture on chlorine to produce argon subject to radioactive decay. The 1968 paper reported an upper limit, rather than a resolved positive signal.[ref]
The underground target contained tetrachloroethylene. Circulated helium swept out argon, which was trapped on cooled charcoal, purified, and put into tiny proportional counters. Electron capture back to chlorine supplies the delayed readout. Added stable argon checked extraction recovery; background counting checked spurious pulses. The capture threshold is 0.814MeV and the product's half-life is about 35 days. The chemical extraction retains neither the original neutrino's arrival time nor its direction.[ref]
The reaction selects electron neutrinos, and its threshold excludes the lowest-energy part of the solar neutrino spectrum. A low count alone cannot distinguish a low source neutrino flux, a changed neutrino flavor mixture, or an underestimated loss in extraction or counting. This is why chemical recovery tests and an independent water Cherenkov neutrino reconstruction are scientifically valuable.
Radiochemical neutrino counting model (μs​=ϵηλR​(1−e−λT)e−λd(1−e−λW))
Words: 274
Homestake experiment OurBigBook.com
An idealized radiochemical neutrino counting model separates production, survival, recovery and readout. Suppose a freshly cleared target produces atoms at a constant rate R during exposure T. Each atom has nuclear decay constant λ=log2/h, where h is its half-life. The expected surviving population obeys
dtdN​=R−λN,N(0)=0,N(T)=λR​(1−e−λT).
(3)
The proof is to multiply the differential equation by eλt and apply integration. The expression also follows by summing the exponential decay survival probabilities of atoms produced at every earlier time. Production does not imply eventual recovery: atoms can decay during exposure.
Let η be the fraction recovered instantaneously at extraction, d the subsequent delay before counting, ϵ the probability of recording a decay, and W the counting duration. The expected signal pulses are
μs​=ϵηN(T)e−λd(1−e−λW).
(4)
With constant background rate b, the expected total is μ=μs​+bW. During counting, the expected instantaneous pulse rate is s(t)+b, with s(t)=ϵηλN(T)e−λ(d+t). Equal time windows therefore lose signal by the factor e−λΔt while a constant background stays unchanged. Fitting the time dependence helps distinguish radioactive decay from that background; it does not recover individual capture times.
For an original worked example choose Rh=20, T=W=h, d=0, η=0.8, ϵ=0.5 and bh=0.2. These are illustrative assumptions. Then N(T)=10/log2, and
μs​=log22​≃2.8854,μ≃3.0854.
(5)
Doubling the exposure does not double the surviving inventory: N(2h)/N(h)=3/2. A delay of one half-life halves the signal. At λT≪1, N(T)≃RT; at long exposure it saturates at R/λ. These limits explain why a large target and repeated extraction can matter more than simply waiting longer. The model neglects time-dependent production, finite extraction duration, residual atoms between runs and time-dependent backgrounds.

A satisfactory solar dynamo model must account for polarity reversal, equatorward activity-belt migration in the solar butterfly diagram, the phase relation between polar and active-region fields, and long-term modulation including solar grand minima.

Bethe stellar energy-production theory

Words: 382
Stellar nuclear fusion OurBigBook.com
Why can a star shine for so long, and why do hotter stellar cores favor different nuclear reactions? A useful theory must supply both an adequate energy reservoir and the right stellar energy-generation rate. Nuclear binding energy supplies the reservoir; the thermonuclear reaction rate, stellar composition and stellar structure determine how quickly it is spent. The proton–proton chain and CNO cycle are two routes for hydrogen burning with very different temperature sensitivities.
In his 1967 lecture, Hans Albrecht Bethe contrasted the short Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time with long ages inferred from terrestrial and stellar evidence.[ref]
For an original solar-scale estimate, choose mass M=1.99×1030kg, radius R=6.96×108m and luminosity L=3.83×1026W. The characteristic Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time GM2/(RL) is about 31Myr; the precise gravitational reservoir has a structure-dependent coefficient. If a fraction f=0.10 of the mass can burn its initial hydrogen mass fraction X=0.70, with a chosen rest-energy conversion fraction η=0.007, the fuel estimate is
tfuel​≃LηfXMc2​≃7.3Gyr.
(11)
This assumes fixed luminosity and neglects neutrino losses. It demonstrates the reservoir advantage, rather than predicting the Sun's age or its full stellar evolution. Having enough fuel still does not identify a reaction: the fuel must release energy at a rate compatible with hydrostatic equilibrium and radiative transfer.
Hans Albrecht Bethe and Charles Louis Critchfield calculated deuterium formation from two protons in 1938, combining quantum tunnelling with a weak conversion of a proton into a neutron. Their calculated nuclear reaction cross-section was a theoretical input to hydrogen burning.[ref] In 1939, Hans Albrecht Bethe analysed the catalytic carbon–nitrogen route and compared required stellar core temperatures with stellar structure estimates in Table VIII. His reported solar agreement used historical abundance and structure assumptions; it should not be read as a modern demonstration that the CNO cycle dominates the Sun.[ref]
Hans Albrecht Bethe's 1967 lecture credits Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker's independent 1938 carbon–nitrogen cycle discovery, distinguishing it from calculation of rates and temperature dependence.[ref] The 1967 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized Hans Albrecht Bethe's contributions to nuclear reaction theory, especially stellar energy production.[ref]
Laboratory nuclear reaction cross-sections were inputs, not measurements of an artificial star. The 1939 paper converted thick-target yields to nuclear reaction cross-sections using a range–energy relation and tabulated capture data.[ref] A concrete apparatus example is the Cockcroft-Walton lithium disintegration experiment, with an accelerated proton beam, lithium target, zinc sulfide screen and beam-blocking control. Its nuclear reaction differs from both stellar burning routes. The 1967 lecture stresses extrapolation below laboratory access and tests for nearby nuclear levels.[ref]

William Alfred Fowler's 1983 lecture connects laboratory nuclear reaction cross-sections to stellar nucleosynthesis and credits Fred Hoyle's stellar synthesis framework.[ref] This complements Bethe stellar energy-production theory: a fuel reservoir alone cannot predict surviving stellar chemical abundances.
Transient beryllium-8 must capture an alpha particle before dissociation; subsequent electromagnetic decay of the Hoyle state can stabilize carbon-12 despite dominant breakup.

Laboratory evidence for the Hoyle state

Words: 140
Fowler nuclear astrophysics OurBigBook.com
In 1953, David Noel Ferguson Dunbar and collaborators used accelerated deuterons on nitrogen-14, populating carbon-12 through 14N(d,α)12C. Magnetic analysis resolved outgoing alpha particle groups. At 620keV incident energy and laboratory angle 90 degrees, they reported excitation 7.68±0.03MeV, with yield 6% of the 4.43MeV group's yield. The stronger group supplied an internal comparison. The paper's opening explicitly relates the search to Fred Hoyle's abundance argument. This is evidence for a nuclear level from a different entrance reaction than stellar fusion.[ref]
The inference uses energy and momentum conservation: at fixed incident energy and observation angle, more energy retained as carbon-12 excitation leaves less outgoing kinetic energy. A resolved particle group therefore identifies a nuclear level. This laboratory nuclear line supports an input required by a stellar synthesis model. It does not reproduce core helium burning, measure a complete stellar carbon yield, or by itself determine the stabilizing decay probability.

In a dilute thermal helium gas with rapid formation–decay balance of beryllium-8, write its small equilibrium abundance schematically as n8​∝nα2​T−3/2exp[−Δ8​/(kB​T)]. A narrow isolated Hoyle state gives a second-step coefficient proportional to T−3/2exp[−ΔC​/(kB​T)]. Multiplication yields
r3α​∝nα3​T−3exp[−kB​TEr​​],Er​=Δ8​+ΔC​,
(12)
with the stabilizing decay strength absorbed into the coefficient. Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. The two positive offsets count energy relative to their respective entrance thresholds, not relative to the carbon-12 ground state. A resonance enhances capture at the relevant energy; the Boltzmann factor still selects how many encounters reach it. This is a sequential narrow-level approximation with fixed nuclear widths, excluding plasma screening and changes of composition or mass density.
William Alfred Fowler lists the Hoyle state 7.654MeV above the carbon-12 ground state, 0.2875MeV above beryllium-8 plus an alpha particle, and 0.3794MeV above three alpha particles.[ref] Subtraction gives Δ8​=0.0919MeV for the diagram.
Normalize the calculated rate at T0​=108K and Er​=0.3794MeV. Holding alpha particle number density and the decay strength fixed gives the original sensitivity calculation
r(T0​,Er​)r(T,Er​+δE)​=(T0​T​)−3exp[−kB​TEr​+δE​+kB​T0​Er​​].
(13)
At T0​, a deliberately chosen shift δE=+100keV multiplies the rate by 9.12×10−6; −100keV gives 1.10×105. These offsets are hypothetical perturbations, not alternative measured nuclear levels. The reference curve has local temperature exponent of a thermonuclear reaction −3+Er​/(kB​T0​)=41.03: raising temperature by 10% gives a factor 41.12 in this fixed-environment calculation. A real star changes its stellar structure and composition as it burns, so these factors do not directly predict final carbon abundance or a constraint on life.

The astrophysical S factor separates the dominant Coulomb barrier suppression from a charged-particle nuclear reaction cross-section σ(E):

(14)

Factoring out a barrier does not remove all nuclear physics: nuclear levels and reaction mechanisms can still make S(E) vary strongly.
For a dilute nonrelativistic Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution of relative motion, multiplying the relative-energy density by speed and nuclear reaction cross-section cancels the explicit factors of E, giving

Proton–proton chain OurBigBook.com
The proton–proton chain first produces deuterium by a weak reaction and then helium-3 by proton capture. pp I ends with 3He+3He→4He+2p. pp II passes through beryllium-7 electron capture to lithium-7 and then proton capture. pp III passes through boron-8 beta-plus decay and beryllium-8 breakup. Each branch produces one net helium-4 nucleus from four protons, but the neutrino spectrum and deposited heat differ. In pp II the net weak reactions involve one emitted positron and one captured electron.

Still farther out its production becomes weak, leaving a smaller envelope abundance. Convective mixing tends to flatten the outer profiles. This qualitative pattern is not itself a quantitative solar model.

Evolutionary tracks on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram connect the central-star temperature and luminosity with core mass and elapsed time.

If a fraction f of a star's mass M supplies fuel abundance X and released energy per unit fuel mass EH​, hydrogen burning gives tnuc​∼fXMEH​/L. This is longer than a structural Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time when the nuclear reservoir greatly exceeds the gravitational contraction reservoir.

A stellar remnant is the object left after a star finishes its principal nuclear-burning evolution, such as a white dwarf, neutron star or black hole. Stellar remnants retain mass while often contributing little optical light, affecting an old stellar population's mass-to-light ratio.

A dense stellar-scale object such as a white dwarf, neutron star or stellar-mass black hole. accretion releases a large gravitational binding energy per unit mass because the accreting surface or inner orbit is small. A black hole has no material surface, so its radiative yield depends on the accretion flow rather than surface impact.

Stellar age (tage​)

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
The stellar age is the elapsed time since a star formed. A constant number formation rate on a finite interval gives a uniform distribution of present ages if every formed object remains counted, including stellar remnants. An age distribution inferred only from surviving main sequence stars generally differs because their lifetimes depend on mass.

Stellar age OurBigBook.com
A cosmological age must exceed the ages of its oldest stellar populations plus their formation interval. globular cluster ages use the main-sequence turnoff with modeled distances, composition, nuclear rates and stellar transport. Their errors are correlated with these inputs, so a lower age bound must propagate the stellar and distance uncertainties rather than treating an isochrone as an exact clock.[ref]

Estimating astronomical ages from radioactive abundance ratios. A ratio evolves as Q=Q0​e−(λ1​−λ2​)t for decay constants λ1​,λ2​. The initial production ratio and subsequent enrichment or mixing must be constrained; an observed ratio alone does not specify a unique age.

Planetary nebula OurBigBook.com
The spectral energy distribution of a planetary nebula combines hot central-star radiation, nebular free-free/free-bound/two-photon continua, recombination and collisionally excited lines, infrared dust emission and sometimes molecular emission. Ionizing-photon supply, gas thermal/ionization balance, density, composition, geometry and extinction determine their relative strengths. A line-dominated broad-band flux is not by itself a continuum temperature measurement.

Planetary-nebula spectral energy distribution OurBigBook.com
Dust contributes a broad infrared continuum together with composition-dependent vibrational structure. Carbon-rich material may show aromatic bands, while oxygen-rich silicates can show features near 9.7 and 18 micrometres. Grain size, charging, transient heating, optical depth and chemical processing affect these features, so one dust temperature cannot characterize every band carrier.
Nebular free-bound continuum
Words: 56
Planetary-nebula spectral energy distribution OurBigBook.com
A nebular free-bound continuum is emitted when a free electron is captured into a bound atomic level and its excess energy leaves as a photon. The threshold energies produce recombination edges such as the Balmer discontinuity. Its spectrum depends on electron temperature, ionic abundances, capture cross-sections and emission measure; it is distinct from bound-bound recombination lines and free-free bremsstrahlung.

The Zanstra method estimates a central star's effective temperature by comparing its observed nonionizing continuum with the absorbed ionizing-photon rate inferred from nebular recombination lines. If ΦE0​​(T)=∫E0​/h∞​Bν​(T)/(hν)dν, then [Fℓ​/(hνℓ​Fνo​,∗​)][β/αℓeff​]=ΦE0​​(Ts​)/Bνo​​(Ts​) when the line traces the full appropriate ionizing budget. Both the distance and stellar radius cancel. Density inhomogeneity also cancels from the integrated recombination estimate when the coefficient ratio is known; photon leakage, dust and mixed-species transfer can invalidate the simple budget.

A carbon-oxygen core is the product of core helium burning. After central helium exhaustion it has little hydrogen or helium, while helium-rich and hydrogen-rich layers surround it.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
A blue loop is an excursion to higher effective temperature, followed by a return redward, during core helium burning in some evolved stars. Its extent depends on core and envelope structure, composition gradients and mixing. Only loops reaching the Cepheid instability strip produce the associated additional Cepheid variable crossings.

The Hertzsprung gap is a sparsely populated region of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram traversed rapidly by many stars evolving away from the main sequence toward the red giant region.

Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction releases gravitational binding energy as a self-gravitating body cools and shrinks. It powers young stars and giant planets before nuclear burning or degeneracy dominates their thermal evolution.

Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism OurBigBook.com
For a monatomic gas obeying the ideal gas law, the specific internal energy is e=3P/(2ρ). With no stellar nuclear fusion heating, the first law of thermodynamics makes the effective stellar energy-generation rate ϵ=−∂t​e−P∂t​(1/ρ), with the derivatives taken at fixed enclosed mass. Differentiating gives ϵ=−3∂t​P/(2ρ)+5P∂t​ρ/(2ρ2). In a fixed-mass stellar homology Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction, ρ∝R−3 and P∝R−4 at each mass label. Hence ϵ=−3PR˙/(2ρR)>0 when R˙<0. This includes internal energy storage as well as pressure work; using the gravitational potential-energy decrease alone would overestimate the outgoing luminosity.

The intrinsic planetary luminosity Lint​ is the power supplied by interior cooling, contraction, nuclear reactions if present, or internal heating, excluding reflected or passively reradiated stellar light. For fixed mass and no accretion or nuclear source, global conservation of energy gives Lint​=Qdeep​−d(U+Ω)/dt, where Qdeep​ is any additional power deposited in the interior, such as tidal heating or Joule heating. For Qdeep​=0 and a gas-supported quasi-static sphere of fixed specific-heat ratio γ and negligible surface pressure, the stellar virial theorem gives Ω=−3(γ−1)U, hence
Lint​=−3(γ−1)3γ−4​dtdΩ​.
(21)
For a dynamically stable gas-supported model take γ>4/3. For γ=5/3 this is half the gravitational release. Degenerate giants require a different internal energy reservoir; the half-factor is not universal.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
Stellar rejuvenation occurs when mixing brings fresh hydrogen into the core of a mass-gaining or merged main sequence star, making its remaining nuclear lifetime resemble that of a younger star. The amount of rejuvenation depends on the accretor's internal mixing and prior composition.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
A helium star has lost most of its hydrogen-rich envelope and is made predominantly of helium. If massive enough, its core can ignite helium; a lower-mass stripped core instead becomes a helium white dwarf.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
An asymptotic-giant-branch star has an inert carbon-oxygen core surrounded by helium- and hydrogen-burning shells and a deep convective envelope. Alternating shell burning produces thermal pulses and dredge-up, while strong mass loss removes the envelope.

Asymptotic giant branch OurBigBook.com
The fate of an Asymptotic giant branch star depends on whether its envelope is removed before its core reaches the next ignition or instability threshold. The approximate envelope-loss time is tenv​=Menv​/∣M˙∣, while the time to add a required core mass ΔMc​ is tgrow​=ΔMc​/M˙c​. Shell stellar nuclear fusion grows the core; third dredge-up can reduce the net growth. If tenv​≪tgrow​, shell fuel disappears first and a white dwarf remnant is favored. The opposite ordering permits further core growth but does not by itself specify whether carbon burning is stable, explosive, or followed by further evolution. Both rates change with time, so the estimates guide rather than replace a stellar model.

A steady outward radial flow with negligible pressure force conserves v2/2−GM/r. If its speed at a reference radius equals the mechanical escape velocity, this constant is zero and v∝r−1/2. Conservation of mass gives ρ∝r−3/2. An adiabatically evolving ideal gas carried along that leading flow has p∝r−3γ/2 and T∝r−3(γ−1)/2.
Finite specific enthalpy changes the dynamical problem: the full conserved Bernoulli equation is v2/2+h−GM/r=B. At the same boundary mechanical escape speed, B=he​ rather than zero. A warm wind therefore needs its enthalpy and equation of state specified before the explicit ballistic velocity can be replaced by a consistent pressure-driven solution.

A neutron star is a compact stellar remnant whose gravity compresses roughly a stellar mass into a radius of order ten kilometres. Degenerate matter supplies most of its pressure support, while rapid rotation and intense magnetic fields can power observable emission.

A magnetic-equilibrium formula is not valid indefinitely as the exterior magnetosphere shrinks inside the star.

Pulsar

Neutron star OurBigBook.com
A pulsar is a rotating magnetized neutron star whose directed emission is observed as periodic pulses. Rotation supplies the energy of an ordinary radio pulsar.
A pulsar turns stellar rotation into an observable clock: the neutron star's emission can continue while its beam sweeps past the observer only briefly. The pulse spacing measures a repetition period; identifying that period with stellar rotation requires a physical model. The discovery of the first pulsar established a remarkably regular astronomical signal before its engine was understood. Today, pulsar dispersion delay also makes these clocks probes of the intervening interstellar medium.

Discovery of the first pulsar

Pulsar OurBigBook.com
Jocelyn Bell Burnell helped build Antony Hewish's radio telescope for finding compact sources through interplanetary scintillation in the solar wind. Operating it and inspecting its chart recorder output in 1967, she recognized an unusual recurring trace, checked earlier charts, and obtained fast recordings resolving pulses in late November. Her observation, recognition and persistent analysis were indispensable.[ref]
The 1968 paper by Antony Hewish, Jocelyn Bell Burnell (bylined S. J. Bell), J. D. H. Pilkington, P. F. Scott and R. A. Collins reported 1.337s spacing and proposed compact-star oscillations. Its radio telescope had 2,048 full-wave dipole antennas in sixteen rows. Four receivers selected declinations; two array halves formed an east-west interferometer. The 81.5MHz receivers passed 1MHz. Observations used 0.05s receiver time constant and Rapidigraph chart recorder with 0.03s time constant; radio second pips calibrated timing.[ref]
Antony Hewish checked sidereal time recurrence. Jocelyn Bell Burnell recalls that P. F. Scott and R. A. Collins reproduced the pulses with another telescope and receivers, while J. D. H. Pilkington measured pulsar dispersion delay: independent checks of instrument independence and intervening plasma.[ref]
A useful numerical comparison uses the approximate sidereal time day of 1436.07min. Relative to a 1440min schedule, the same sky direction transits about 3.93min earlier each day, or 39.3min after ten days. This compares successive passages through the receiving beam; it is a different clock from the roughly 1.3s pulse spacing within one passage. Sky recurrence alone cannot rule out every transmitter or reflection, and pulsar dispersion delay alone does not uniquely establish an emission mechanism. Their strength lies in independent constraints agreeing.
The discovery lesson is that an unexpected signal must survive changes of readout, instrument and observing date. Increasing chart recorder speed exposed structure hidden in a compressed trace; it did not make the source begin pulsing. The pulsar interpretation now separates the rotating clock, beam geometry, pulsar magnetosphere emission and pulsar dispersion delay. The initial observation established periodic arrival, not a direct measurement of the neutron star's surface motion or radius.

In the ideal unmagnetized limit, the dispersion relation is ω2=c2k2+ωp2​, where ωp​ is the angular plasma frequency. Here f=ω/(2π) is ordinary frequency, e is the magnitude of the elementary charge, me​ is the electron mass, ϵ0​ is the vacuum permittivity, ne​ is electron number density, and c is the speed of light. At Ptrial​=P, all arrivals fold to one phase. But P/2 also puts all arrivals at one phase: folding discarded the fact that alternate proposed cycles contain no pulse. At 2P, the arrivals instead occupy two phases, 0 and 1/2. Thus a sharp folded profile alone need not identify the fundamental period.

For N=100 and Ptrial​=1.401s, this is about −0.07066 cycle. Splitting the observation into early and late pieces reveals the drift that one full folded average can blur. Separately, regular discrete sampling can create aliasing: observing at a spacing comparable with the pulse width can miss narrow pulses even when the recurrence period is much longer. White dwarf

Words: 1k Articles: 19
Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
A white dwarf is a compact stellar remnant supported mainly by electron degeneracy pressure. Its ions carry most of the mass, while its electrons provide most of the supporting pressure. The Pauli exclusion principle makes compression fill quantum states with larger momenta; support therefore persists even when thermal motion becomes small. Cooling and hydrostatic equilibrium are separate questions: a white dwarf can radiate stored energy while retaining degeneracy support.
The surprising trend is that a more massive cold white dwarf is smaller. Its higher mass density raises the Fermi momentum, eventually requiring special relativity. The degenerate-electron pressure crossover explains why this response approaches a limiting stiffness and why the Chandrasekhar limit exists. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's 1983 lecture develops this connection between quantum statistics, stellar structure and stellar evolution.[ref]

Chandrasekhar limit

Words: 420 Articles: 2
White dwarf OurBigBook.com
The Chandrasekhar mass is the limiting mass of a cold nonrotating white dwarf supported by relativistic electron degeneracy pressure, about 1.4M⊙​ for ordinary composition. It bounds the retained remnant's mass, rather than the birth mass of a star that can lose an envelope. The ideal limit assumes fixed mean molecular weight per electron, Newtonian gravity and a noninteracting degenerate electron gas; electron capture, general relativity, stellar rotation and ignition can change the attainable endpoint.
The Chandrasekhar limit belongs to work of the early 1930s. In his 1983 retrospective, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar reprints the 1935 mass–radius sequence and then discusses stellar evolution and relativistic stability.[ref] The 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized his broader theoretical work on stellar structure and stellar evolution; the other half recognized William Alfred Fowler's theoretical and experimental work on nuclear reactions underlying chemical element formation.[ref]

Binary star OurBigBook.com
An X-ray binary has a compact mass-gaining star or black hole accreting from a companion, so that much of its emitted power appears as X-rays. Gravitational binding energy supplies an accretion luminosity of order GMM˙/R when there is a surface or an appropriate inner disk radius. The donor star may feed an accretion disk through Roche-lobe overflow or a stellar wind.

X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
An ultraluminous X-ray source is an apparently off-nuclear compact X-ray source with inferred isotropic luminosity above roughly 1032 W. Luminosity alone does not establish an intermediate-mass black hole: supercritical accretion, beaming and magnetized neutron-star accretion can also produce large apparent luminosities. Spatial association, spectra, timing and dynamical constraints help distinguish models.

X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
A binary in which a black hole captures part of its companion's stellar wind. The captured gas can dissipate energy and, with sufficient specific angular momentum, form an accretion disk. A stellar black-hole binary with a massive stellar companion. A 2011 dynamical analysis combined optical photometry and spectroscopy with a distance constraint and inferred 14.8±1.0 solar masses for the compact object. This is that study's historical estimate, not a claim about the latest measurement.[ref]

Words: 49
X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
A Type I X-ray burst is a transient thermonuclear runaway in accreted hydrogen or helium on a neutron star surface. It rises rapidly and cools after the fuel burns. A black hole has no material surface on which the same accumulated surface-fuel event can occur. This is distinct from an accretion-powered X-ray pulse or an accretion instability.

X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
An accreting X-ray pulsar contains a magnetized neutron star whose magnetic field channels the accreting gas toward its magnetic poles. Rotation carries the bright accretion regions through the observer's view and produces pulses. The input angular momentum can change the spin period; this differs from the rotational energy source of an isolated pulsar.

X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
A high-mass X-ray binary has a massive donor star supplying an accreting neutron star or black hole. A strong stellar wind often feeds it, although Roche-lobe overflow and donor equatorial outflows also occur. The short lifetime of the donor associates these systems with young stellar populations.

X-ray binary OurBigBook.com
In a low-mass X-ray binary, the donor star is relatively low mass. Roche-lobe overflow usually feeds an accretion disk around a neutron star or black hole. The low-mass label concerns the donor rather than the total binary mass. Accumulated fuel on a neutron star can produce a Type I X-ray burst.

Binary star OurBigBook.com
A detached binary has both components lying inside their respective Roche lobes, so neither currently transfers matter by Roche-lobe overflow. A detached system may still exchange matter through a stellar wind.

Coeval binary population

Words: 241 Articles: 3
Binary star OurBigBook.com
A coeval binary has components formed at the same time. A population of such binary stars can still have a distribution of system ages. If component masses have independence and the state at age t is determined separately for each component, the states have conditional independence given t. If g(t) and w(t) are the conditional probabilities of two states, the unconditional unordered pair fractions are E[g(t)2] and 2E[g(t)w(t)], not generally products of marginal state fractions.

Suppose binary ages have uniform coordinate y∈[0,1] and independently sampled component masses give disjoint conditional state fractions g(y)=ay and w(y)=by. Integrating the conditional pair probabilities gives P(GG)=a2/3, P(GW)=2ab/3, and P(WW)=b2/3. The fraction with at least one G is a−a2/3, and the fraction of those systems with a second evolved component is (a2+2ab)/(3a−a2). Components share their age, so their unconditional states are correlated even when their birth masses have independence.

Pre-giant Roche-lobe-filling period limit OurBigBook.com
For fixed total solar-unit mass m and conserved orbital angular momentum, conservative binary mass transfer preserves K=P[md​(m−md​)]3. Hence P/md2​=K/[md5​(m−md​)3]. Its logarithmic derivative is −5/md​+3/(m−md​), vanishing at 5m/8 with positive second derivative. The ratio diverges at both endpoints, so this is its global minimum. Comparing this minimum to a pre-giant bound P0​ tests whether any such conservative antecedent can overflow before the giant branch; satisfying it is necessary, not a proof of an entire evolutionary history.

Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
In nonconservative binary evolution, matter can escape the system and/or external processes change its orbital angular momentum. Escaping overflow, a stellar wind and a common envelope can invalidate the fixed-total-mass and period-product invariants of conservative mass transfer.

An isotropic escaping stellar wind has the donor star's mean specific orbital angular momentum. With M˙d​<0, retained fraction f, negligible spin and no additional wind torque, J˙=(1−f)M˙d​ad2​Ω. The retained matter redistributes angular momentum internally. Unlike isotropic re-emission from a binary star, the escaping material originates at the donor rather than the accretor. With no retention this reduces to Jeans-mode mass loss.

Donor-wind Roche-lobe response OurBigBook.com
A donor star with stellar radius response exponent ζ∗​ can maintain exact contact in the donor-wind Roche-lobe response model for some retained fraction 0≤f≤1 precisely when ζ∗​ lies between ζ0​ and ζ1​. This follows because the attainable Roche-lobe radius response exponents form that closed interval. If its endpoints coincide, all fractions work when ζ∗​ equals the common value and none work otherwise. With negative donor mass-loss rate, dlog(Rd​/RL​)/dt=(ζ∗​−ζL​)M˙d​/Md​ distinguishes detachment from increasing overfill. Dynamical stability of binary mass transfer requires the adiabatic donor response.

For a slowly evolving circular orbit with constant retained fraction f and donor-wind angular-momentum loss, logarithmic differentiation of the circular-binary orbital angular momentum gives dlogP=−3fdlogMd​−3dlogMa​−2dlog(Md​+Ma​). Integration gives the displayed invariant. At f=1 it becomes the period-product invariant for conservative mass transfer, while at f=0 it becomes PM2=constant. A varying retained fraction does not give this simple power-law invariant.
Case B mass transfer
Words: 71 Articles: 1
Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
Case B mass transfer starts after core hydrogen exhaustion and before core helium ignition. It is subdivided by donor structure; early case B mass transfer occurs before a deep convective giant envelope develops.
Early case B mass transfer
Words: 43
Case B mass transfer OurBigBook.com
Early case B overflow occurs in an early post-main-sequence donor, commonly crossing the Hertzsprung gap with a largely radiative envelope. A stabilizing mass-loss response can allow transfer at binary mass ratios that would destabilize a convective giant. This is an evolutionary-stage classification, distinct from recombination terminology.
Case A mass transfer
Words: 27
Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
Case A mass transfer starts while the donor star is on the main sequence, with core hydrogen burning. Its onset precedes giant-envelope formation; donor structure and the binary mass ratio still determine stability.

Negligible spin and a circular orbit give J=M1​M2​Ga/M​. Fixed M and J imply a(M1​M2​)2 is constant. Kepler's third law then gives the period-product invariant P(M1​M2​)3.

Period-product invariant for conservative mass transfer OurBigBook.com
At fixed total mass M and period-product invariant, P/Md2​ is proportional to [Md5​(M−Md​)3]−1. Its unique global minimum occurs at donor mass 5M/8 and accretor mass 3M/8. It is useful for testing all possible conservative progenitors against a pre-overflow period bound.
Dynamical stability of binary mass transfer

Conservative binary mass transfer OurBigBook.com
Binary mass transfer is dynamically stable when the donor's radius decreases relative to its Roche-lobe radius after a small mass loss, reducing overflow instead of amplifying it.

Dynamical stability of binary mass transfer OurBigBook.com
With fixed total mass and orbital angular momentum and RL​∝a(Md​/M)1/3, the Roche-lobe radius response exponent is 2q−5/3. A donor with stellar radius response exponent ζ∗​ is stable to infinitesimal mass loss when ζ∗​>2q−5/3, giving q<(ζ∗​+5/3)/2. The threshold depends on the donor response.
Stellar radius response exponent (ζ=dlogR/dlogM)
Words: 48
Dynamical stability of binary mass transfer OurBigBook.com
The stellar radius response exponent measures how a star's radius changes as it loses mass. The adiabatic exponent ζad​ describes loss too rapid for thermal adjustment; the equilibrium exponent ζeq​ follows a sequence of thermally relaxed stars. Compare ζad​ with the Roche-lobe radius response exponent to test dynamical stability.

Let q=M1​/M2​, hold total binary mass fixed, use RL​∝aq3/10, and impose dlogJ=fdlogM1​. The circular-binary orbital angular momentum then gives dloga/dlogM1​=2(q−1+f), whereas mass conservation gives dlogq/dlogM1​=1+q. Thus ζL​=(23q−17+20f)/10. If the donor obeys R1​=KM1β​ with slowly varying K, loss of donor mass increases its overfill when ζL​>β, or q>(17−20f+10β)/23. This is a feedback criterion on the time scale of the assumed donor response, not automatically a dynamical instability for every choice of β. For β=1/2, the threshold is (22−20f)/23; if f≥11/10, every positive mass ratio satisfies it.
White-dwarf mass--orbital-period relation
Words: 43
Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
Stable envelope stripping of a low-mass red giant leaves a helium white dwarf. Because the giant radius is determined mainly by its core mass and fixes its Roche-lobe radius at detachment, the final binary orbital period is tightly related to the white-dwarf mass.
Common envelope
Words: 109 Articles: 2
Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
A common-envelope phase occurs when unstable binary interaction engulfs both stellar cores in one envelope. Orbital energy and angular momentum may eject the envelope, leaving a compact binary, or the cores may merge.
Common-envelope energy formalism
Words: 41
Common envelope OurBigBook.com
The common-envelope energy formalism equates a fraction αCE​ of the released orbital energy to the envelope binding energy, often written Ebind​=GMd​Menv​/(λRd​). It estimates the post-envelope separation but compresses uncertain hydrodynamics into αCE​ and λ.
Double-degenerate Type Ia supernova scenario
Words: 35
Common envelope OurBigBook.com
The double-degenerate scenario forms a close pair of carbon--oxygen white dwarfs, usually through mass transfer and one or more common-envelope phases. Gravitational radiation then shrinks the orbit until merger or unstable transfer triggers thermonuclear disruption.
Algol binary
Words: 192 Articles: 3
Roche-lobe overflow OurBigBook.com
An Algol binary is a semidetached binary in which an evolved, less massive donor star fills its Roche lobe while its more massive mass gainer remains near the main sequence. Binary mass-ratio reversal resolves the Algol paradox. Eclipsing members commonly have Algol variable light curves, but that observational class also includes detached systems.
Algol paradox
Words: 41
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
The Algol paradox is the apparently inconsistent evolutionary ordering in an Algol binary: the less massive star is more evolved, whereas higher-mass isolated main sequence stars normally exhaust core fuel sooner. Binary mass-ratio reversal resolves it by identifying the present donor as the initially more massive star.
Binary mass-ratio reversal
Words: 50
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
During binary mass-ratio reversal, an initially more massive donor star loses enough material that its companion becomes the more massive member. The stars retain their different prior nuclear evolution, resolving the Algol paradox. Conservative binary mass transfer shrinks the orbit before equal masses and widens it after reversal, because a∝(Md​Ma​)−2 at fixed total mass and orbital angular momentum.
Algol mass-ratio stability limit (qcrit​≃2/3)
Words: 63
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
A simplified conservative model with a fully convective donor gives long-lived stable Roche-lobe overflow only for donor-to-accretor mass ratio q<2/3. This follows from the Roche-lobe radius response exponent and the donor's adiabatic stellar radius response exponent −1/3. The boundary is model-dependent; radiative donors, evolved core structure and mass or angular-momentum loss change it. Van Rensbergen and collaborators' Algol population study includes reported Algol mass ratios above 0.7 and discusses observational uncertainties.
